utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the following two witnesses are witnesses through whom the Prosecution seeks to tender huge, huge batches of documents, primarily post mortem reports, post mortem examination reports. In the normal scheme of things, these might well be documents that would be agreed, but we have been moving so fast, admirably, but we have not been in a position in which we could discuss them in detail with the Defence. The Prosecution, however, would, I think, have a duty at some stage to make this massive material, documents numbering in the thousands, intelligible to the Court. And it is our intention, in due course, to present to the Court an explanatory document, a demonstratory that can link the various bits of pieces and evidence related to persons identified in the schedules which are in various batches of these documents and link them in one document. In other words, the evidence would be more intelligible if there was some system. I intend to introduce to the Court a system, a demonstrated system, where the individual victims of the schedules could be linked to those documents, the individual crime sites which are relevant to the case could be linked to those documents, and the individual -- well, the documents relating to various municipalities insofar as they could be linked. We intend to do so when the -- when we tender the remainder of the evidence, because there would be more, in particular some DNA evidence in respect to these bodies. This is something that was ordered, I think, in the Milosevic case, and I think it was -- it is the appropriate way to go. And we propose to do so because I think there would be some difficulty in going through so much material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't get the impression, from reading these statements, that there were ongoing DNA investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the DNA investigations were completed in July of this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why do you say, when we tender the remainder of the evidence, there would be more, in particular some DNA evidence in respect of those?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These witnesses, although they did use the results of the DNA evidence, they did not participate in the DNA examinations. We would need to tender the DNA -- unless it is agreed, we need to tender the DNA evidence through another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's difficult to understand why this wasn't done in the pre-trial phase of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Much of the evidence in respect to the DNA had been ongoing for some time, and there were also problems, which eventually the Court will become aware when we call these witnesses, if we need to call these witnesses, in getting the witness, in physically getting the witness, because of some work-related issues. However, I do concede that in respect to whether or not discussions could be had in respect to these documents, perhaps at least the post mortem examination reports might have been considered for discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But at this moment, is there any useful purpose to be served by leading these witnesses in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Their statements and the reports they tender explain the procedures that they applied, the methodologies they applied, and the batches of post mortem examination reports have the results of the procedures and methodologies that they applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, well, that can all -- I can read that here, but what useful purpose is listening to these witnesses going to serve in relation to what you describe as a massive documentation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The witnesses, as you can read, they provide a nexus between the exhumation of the bodies and the post mortem reports and their eventual handover to UNMIK for repatriation, UNMIK being the United Nations Mission in Kosovo. The evidence would have to be heard in the absence of an order -- it is my submission there would need to be some evidence authenticating these documents, explaining, at least to a limited degree, how they were created, unless there is an order under Rule 92 bis that they could be received through cross-examination without the witness attending or unless there is agreement, which perhaps is the way to go. But it is true, Your Honour, that, even in speaking with these witnesses, if they are asked anything in any real detail about the material, they would open the documents and look at the documents because there's just so much it's really beyond human memory. So the documents themselves speak -- the documents speak for themselves. But we did need to lay a foundation to tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. O'Sullivan, are you able to assist on the degree that you anticipate these witnesses will be cross-examined?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I expect they'll be cross-examined very little, Your Honour, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The ideal situation, I think, would have been, if there was a summary report in relation to the work done which tied the bodies examined to the indictment, and once that was available, the witnesses were here to be cross-examined to the extent that there was some challenge to that. We note what you say about what you plan, Mr. Stamp, but it's a pity it wasn't planned at a much earlier stage in the case, and then perhaps updated if there was further work ongoing. But it's been known, it would appear, since 2001 that these were sites with -- potentially the resting place of the -- final resting place of victims of events in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Not that it makes much of a difference to the gravamen of what you have just said, but the exhumations continued into 2002, 2003, and the identifications continued on an ongoing basis right up until early this year. But it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll be interested to hear what questions you can ask either of these witnesses that will meaningfully expand upon what's set out in the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I really will ask some questions to authenticate the documents. There's not much I have to ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But have they not done that in the statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To some degree, Your Honour. I was hoping that if I do ask them some questions, it might make the batch of documents more easier to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, all right. Let's hear from the first one. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's Professor Dusan Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. It might be best if you close the book for the moment until we see if any reference to your own documentation is necessary. We are already in possession of a statement which refers to an enormous amount of documentation which is already here in some form. It's not clear to me exactly what you will be asked about, and therefore I can't give you much guidance since it's up to the parties what questions they're going to ask you. Now, the first person to ask you in this instance will be for the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor. Firstly, could you just state your name, tell us your profession, and what your present job occupation is.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I am Professor Dusan Dunjic, Professor at the Medical School of the University of Belgrade, and I work at the Institute of Forensic Medicine. I'm a full-time professor, teaching forensic medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in 2001, what was your job posting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In 2001, in end May/early June, I was invited by the president of the district court in Belgrade, Mrs. Vida Petrovic-Kero, to come together with the district prosecutor in Belgrade, Mr. Terzic, to reach an agreement about going out to the location of Batajnica, which was suspected to contain a mass grave with a large number of bodies in it. As a professor of forensic medicine, at that time head of the institute, I had, under order of the court, to organise the exhumation of those bodies and make sure that all measures are taken to identify them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were then head of the institute. In respect to the work you did at Batajnica, did you give a statement to the OTP on the 9th to the 11th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. In respect to the exhumations and work you conducted at Batajnica, did you give a statement to an investigator from the OTP on the 11th of May, 2006, this year?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did give a statement. I meant the prosecutor's office in Belgrade and you mean the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. Yes, I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That statement is P2389, Your Honours. I tender it and ask that it be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of that statement, you refer - and you just referred, as well - to an order given by the judge. I would like to show you that order, which is P2396.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could that be brought up? Could you scroll down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As you see, the stamp and the signature of the investigating judge, Goran Cavlina.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document that we received at the Institute of Forensic Medicine, ordering the establishment of a team to conduct this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, at paragraph 12 of the statement, there is a list of documents, including the one which the witness was just shown. These documents are in e-court as P2395 to P2406. Without going through all of those documents, I propose to tender them, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, just before moving on. In relation -- these relate to Batajnica 1, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to Batajnica 2, there is actually a summary report, I think; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is a summary report in respect to both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Both. And what number is the summary report for Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For Batajnica 1, it's P168. I was just coming to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the numbers you've just given us are 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that there are 12 bodies, apparently?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. These are 12 documents which are referred to in paragraph 12 of his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But is there one for each of 12 bodies, or is it something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, it's something else. These are individual documents dealing with individual aspects of the exhumations. The forensic reports, the batch of forensic reports, is Exhibit P2407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I -- yes, I see -- my confusion -- sorry, Mr. Stamp, it's my fault, but there are two paragraph 12s in your report and I'm looking at the second one when I should have been looking -- in the statement, when I should have been looking at the first one. And now I follow it more clearly. But it would help if we confined ourselves to numbering each paragraph consecutively.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That had escaped my attention. Thank you very much, Your Honour. Of course I was referring to the first 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I now follow it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to try to take you quickly through some of the documents that are related to your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we look at P159. These are some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What does this photograph depict?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: This photograph has a two-fold meaning. First of all, this is the location Batajnica 1, where we see two tents; one in the right-hand corner covering the pit, and the other tent on the left-hand side of the picture is the tent in which we conducted examinations of the bodies removed from the pit. On the right-hand side is a truck which, in fact, was a water tank, which provided us with running water, and the white truck is a refrigerator truck where we kept the bodies after they were examined and autopsied. And that refrigerator truck was there the whole time while we were working at Batajnica. That is to explain the photograph itself. But another thing that I should point out here is this water you can see. It was a very rainy period in early June when we had to suspend the exhumations for a while, for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we flip to the last photograph in that series on P159. May I just indicate, Your Honours, there is an index of these photographs, which is P158. This exhibit is P159. The index indicates that this is a view of the exhumation site following the initial ground clearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you describe, very briefly, what's in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: On this photograph that was taken from the north-eastern side, that is, looking from the tent that covers the whole pit, we see the area where the bodies were located, the bodies we found later. This photograph shows the rain-water from the rainfalls that came earlier and that covered our first excavations in the area. After this water was removed, we found bodies in the central part of this pit, the bodies that we can see on other photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have up P168. Your Honours, at paragraph 4 of the statement, the witness refers to his report on the exhumation, his overview report of the exhumation, and that is a document which has been brought.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's page 9 of this report, a working diary where we would describe the body parts that we found, in which area we found them, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I'd just like to take you to one or two parts of the report, just to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: First, could we look at the last page of the report? It has just been pointed out to me that the document is -- there is an error in the ERN ending, in the numbering. So it is the third page on e-court. Actually, the last page of the report is the third page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is where you -- that is your signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's my signature of the 5th of July, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You detail in the reports -- in the report the procedure you applied in exhuming these bodies and conducting the post mortem examination reports. So I will just take you to one or two sections of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the English version, at page 2. Again, because of the difficulty with the B/C/S version in e-court, I wonder if he could be handed a hard copy of this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the middle of page 2 you describe the labelling of the bodies, the labelling of the bodies and body parts and items and effects found in the excavation. "It was agreed that all body parts and bodies would be labelled BA and given a number from 1 upward. Additionally, all loose clothing was given the label 'BASG' and a number, and loose items found were given the label 'BAP' and a number." Now, can I just ask you one thing about the numbering. What would be done with artefacts that were found, including that was on a body?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The agreement we had was as follows: That all objects found on the body or with the body, together with the clothing, should be recorded in the autopsy referring to that body and given a certain number; however, there were objects that fell outside that category, although they were found in the same location, and they would be given -- they would be given an indication, a mark, "PA," for object. The objects found in pockets or on the body of the victim would be given the same reference number as the victim.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: All valuables, such as jewellery and money, were later handed over to the investigating judge for the safe-keeping of the court, and they were later used for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. So personal items and effects found on the body, the clothing on the body, would be given the same number as the body?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Let me just add. In addition to this description given in the autopsy report, we photographed the objects and the photographs were given the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I indicated, P2407 is the batch, huge batch, of exhumation reports. Because of difficulties in uploading -- not in uploading but in referring to various documents within the batch, we have taken some of them out -- not taken some of them out. We have reproduced some of them with separate exhibit numbers, Your Honours, so that -- for ease of reference. And these are P169 to 188. These are individual reports for some of the victims who were later identified by DNA exhibits. I'd quickly like to just have a look at -- I don't intend to go through all of them, just one of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you do that, are these exhibits which are in addition to the ones referred to in the written statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where do I find 2407 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in the written statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, Your Honour. That is the second paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's 2407?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And the photographs P159, where do we find them in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: P159, photos of examined -- I do not believe that they are specifically referred to in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the same would be the case with the index, P158?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thanks. Professor, is it possible to say the number of persons of whom parts were found in Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the report that we made and that was officially published, signed by the president of the district court in Belgrade, we said that at the Batajnica 1 location at least 36 human corpses were found of both genders and of different age groups. We also indicated that out of those 36, nine were established to be younger than seven. One child's corpse had the intrauterine age of eight months. Other remains, such as individual bones, were also examined and processed and also marked with the same "BA" reference, together with the number, but those individual bones were impossible to fit anthropologically with the whole corpses that we had. That's why we said we had found at least 36 bodies. And we can only assume that among the other remains there was a body of maybe another person. Out of the whole bodies, the bodies -- or the remains that we could establish to belong to one person, we took bone samples for future DNA analysis. However, we also took bone samples for DNA analysis from the remains that we did not integrate with whole corpses, and that's how we were able to establish the identities of the persons. And, indeed, we reached the number of at least 36 in Batajnica 1. I'm sorry. When we received DNA reports for Batajnica 1, it turned out that three different bone samples - one arm, one leg, another leg - according to the DNA analysis, belonged to one person. And then we were able to put together one whole body, or most of it, that belongs to one person and join it with some other separate bones found in the same location marked with different numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Stamp, is that report by the president of the district court already in process?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not. Is it likely to come or is it a separate -- a matter that we are not to be concerned with?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: A matter that I don't think you need to be concerned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That aspect in respect to the bodies and the DNA analysis we expect to be dealt with by the persons who dealt with the taking of the DNA samples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And may I just indicate, without going through those documents, that in those -- among the batch of 12 documents referred to in the first paragraph 12 of this statement, there is P2402, which is a chart of the examination of body parts, loose body parts; and P2403, which is a chart of the examination -- in respect to the examination of the 36 body parts which he just mentioned. I would have asked him about that, but since he referred to that, I don't think there's any need to open those exhibits and explain what's in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was indicating, Your Honour, P1691, in it are samples, just samples, of some forensic reports which are in the batch P2407, and these are some of those people who were later identified by DNA. I just want to have a look at one of them and ask him three questions about it. Could we look at P182 as a sample from the sample. Could we quickly go to the last page -- or could we scroll page by page to the last page. There are only four pages. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see at the bottom of -- well, firstly, is that the standard format of your post mortem examination reports for the remains that you examined? And do you see there on the last page your signature and the signature of your colleagues for that report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a post mortem report that contains all the relevant data established on the spot through exhumation, autopsy, and anthropological examination of individual bones. After the autopsy findings, a conclusion is given at the end, and below the conclusion all members of the commission involved in this case put their signatures, the whole team. The first signature below the words "Commission of Forensic Medical Doctors" is my signature, and the other signatures are those of my associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While we're on that page, if you have a look at conclusion number 3, Professor, I wish to ask you about it because it appears in many of these reports -- sorry, conclusion -- yes, number 3, firstly. The autopsy reveals that certain parts of the body had been exposed to high temperatures, like fire. Was this a rare observation, or did most of the bodies indicate that there had been an attempt to burn them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. There is an objection to this question. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think the last part of that question, "Was this a rare observation, or did most of the bodies indicate that there had been an attempt to burn them" goes way beyond anything contained in that report and is leading and argumentative on the part of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I agree with my friend, but I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's not what the conclusion says. You're way beyond what's already there, so I think you better start that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You say here, Professor, that the autopsy reveals that certain parts of the body had been exposed to high temperature, fire. What did that indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Should I provide an answer as a witness or as an expert? As a witness, this would mean that by carrying out autopsies, the presence of high temperature, that is fire, was established and its traces on the bones. As to how that came about and under what circumstances and at what time, well, that part I need to answer as an expert and I do believe that I'm here as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you answer the question as an expert, based on your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I mean, this was dealt with last May at a 65 ter where we requested whether these people -- whether this witness and the other one were testifying as fact witnesses or as experts, and it was clearly determined that they were fact. There's been no expert report and they were not presented to us as expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there's no report by the witness, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, no report filed under Rule 94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but any report under any rule saying what his conclusions are about what happened to cause the damage that you're now referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no, there is no such report. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in these circumstances, we will consider the position. Just give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because this issue was specifically addressed in the pre-trial stage, we do not consider the question that's just been asked to be admissible. However, there can be grey areas in relation to witnesses such as this, who are clearly experts on any view of matters and, even in dealing with issues of fact, bring to bear inevitably the expertise of learning and experience. So we're not saying that questions of this nature would always be inadmissible to a witness who doesn't come clearly labelled as an expert witness in advance. But where the matter's been addressed specifically in the pre-trial stage, there does seem, to us, to be force in the objection and, therefore, we exclude expert -- at least we find the question asked inadmissible. I think, Mr. Stamp, that this chapter started as an attempt to find out how widespread the fire damage was, and that's obviously a matter that the witness can deal with, but there must be certain limitations in the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Based on your observations of these remains, were many of them or just a few of them indicating signs that they had been burnt, from what you saw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is the same question but in different words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the way it's -- the way it's put may not be ideal, but all this question relates to is whether there were signs of damage by fire, not how that fire may have been caused, which is the area that has been excluded. So the question is confined --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not what we received in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question specifically to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Otherwise, this is the best expert we have in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, the question you are being asked is: How widespread were your findings of damage by fire on the bodies examined from Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be able to provide a specific answer to this specific question, I would have to go through each and every report from Batajnica 1. This particular case, Batajnica 20 -- well, I don't know the exact number. Could we please go back to page 1. 22. In this report, in this autopsy finding, we have a detailed description of "the parts of bones and skeleton suffered damage from high temperature." And this applies to each and every case for which we have autopsy reports and findings for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, the material's all there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it doesn't look as though exploring it in court is the most efficient way of dealing with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, no. I'm trying to avoid having to go through all these documents. We are on P182. Is that before the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that is the document which is presently before him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we go back to that last page of the document. Your Honour, with your leave, may I move on from that document, because it does not indicate what my notes have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would like P139. And while it comes up, P139 to 156 are samples from the exhumation reports involving photos and indices for these photos of the human remains as well as personal effects that were recovered. Could we have a look at page 9 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is this an example of the identification documents that were found in clothing on some of these bodies and that were recorded -- photographed and recorded in your examination -- sorry, in your post mortem examination reports?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a personal document, or rather, this is a photograph of this person's ID which had been found on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just for the record, this document refers to Afrim Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Lastly, in respect to Batajnica 1, Professor, could we have a look at P167.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. P167, Your Honour, are a set of photographs of the grave-site after it had been exhumed -- after it had been excavated, I'm sorry, and P166 is an index of those photographs. Is -- very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there a problem, Riaz, about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the last -- on the next-to-last photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That looks like the index rather than the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, this is P166, the index; the photographs are P167. Could we look at the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is that the condition of the excavation -- the pit, the grave, after it had been exhumed and cleaned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This photograph was taken after all the corpses and objects had been taken out. On this photograph you can see four parallel beams. These are sleepers for trams, tram tracks. We have a shorter beam and another one which is perpendicular to the four parallel ones. All of them were carbonised.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And they were found at the bottom of the pit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Among the persons who were members of your examination team, was there an archaeologist by the name of Andrej Starovic, and did he provide a report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I refer to item 11 in the first paragraph 12 of his statement, and that is P2405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, first of all, do we have an answer to the question whether there was an archaeologist called Starovic in your team?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you verbally --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this, you say, is item 11 on the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the first paragraph 12, and it's P2405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could that be brought up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, if I read from it, if, perhaps, you recall what he said about these sleepers. And this is at page 13 of the English version of P2405, and it is in the middle of page K0527227 in the version in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the report specifying the archaeological findings at Batajnica 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll forego reading the report; it speaks for itself. It describes the condition of the pit and the sleepers, as they were discovered in the course of the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is described in detail in this document with all the positions relative to the archaeologically important items.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm nearly done with this witness. If I may just indicate to the Court another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I may just indicate that in respect to Batajnica 2, which is described in this statement at paragraph 13 and thereafter, P2410 is a report on the exhumations at Batajnica 2 referred to in paragraph 13. P942 contains a full batch of reports, and that's a rather large exhibit, of the exhumations at Batajnica 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that the equivalent of 2407 for Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The procedures that you adopted in respect to the exhumation and the preparation of the post mortem reports in respect to your examination of Batajnica 2, later on in 2001, from July 2001, were they the same or approximately the same as those applied to your examinations of Batajnica 1?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The procedure was the same, identical, but the conditions under which we worked were different. Here, I mean that there was a great number of cases and a great number -- and a -- that it was very hot. This made things more difficult. As regards the autopsy and the anthropological analysis, those were identical. It was also followed by a number of x-rays of bones for easier identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned earlier in your evidence that you collected bone samples from the bodies that were exhumed and the body parts that were exhumed. Did you also collect bone samples from the body parts in respect to Batajnica 2 as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. All bone samples that could be matched to individual persons were identified or marked in the same way. As for the loose bones, they were also treated forensically and anthropologically, and those loose bones were collected together and disposed of the way it was described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you mention in -- if I may go very quickly, in paragraph 9 of your statement, that the bone samples in respect to paragraph -- in respect to Batajnica 1 were handed over by you to Dr. Alonso at the National Institute of Toxicology in Madrid. Did you also hand over bone samples in respect to these cases to officials from the International Commission for Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you can tell us very briefly, did you participate in the identification of these bodily remains after you received DNA results from both the toxicology institute in Madrid and also the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the end, when things were concluded, I participated in the identification procedure. It doesn't boil down solely to the use of the DNA profile from individual bones, but it also encompasses the analysis of the autopsy anthropological findings in the form of the autopsy reports you saw, plus the DNA report, which is actually called a DNA profile for that particular bone, as well as antemortem data collected by certain services from the people down in Kosovo who were relatives to the missing persons. Then we tried to match and compare all the data so as to be able to establish whether a given corpse with our identification number belongs to a certain person, to someone with a first and last name. I participated in that process, together with my colleagues, who worked at the exhumation site and who carried out the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And when the bodies were identified, they were handed over -- they were repatriated to Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: After the identification procedure was completed, this being a complex procedure, we made a list of the people who had been identified. After that, through the centre for coordination which had been established in our country, and together with UNMIK, we had an agreement with these two offices by which those people were to be -- or the corpses were to be repatriated to Kosovo and handed over to their relatives who identified them. The repatriation process was ongoing until recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: "Recently" meaning in the last few months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing further in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. To clarify the position with regard to exhibits, all referred to will be admitted, and, for the avoidance of doubt, the ones which have simply been identified by number and not referred to in any detail, that that applies to are P2395 to 2406, P168, P169 to 188, P139 to 156, P2410, and P942. The others were dealt -- in fact, one or two of those I just mentioned were referred to also clearly, and there are -- the others which were referred to are also admitted. Now, Professor, we need to have a break at this stage to allow interpreters to recover for the next stage of the proceedings. That's normally 20 minutes. We'll resume at 4.15, and meanwhile you'll be shown where to wait by the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first will be counsel for General Lukic and thereafter we'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Professor Dunjic. My name is Branko Lukic and, together with my colleagues, I appear today for General Lukic before this Tribunal. First of all, I will follow up on several questions asked of you by my learned friend, Mr. Stamp, and then we will go on to the topic of the lake which hasn't been mentioned but we can find it in your statements.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when did you receive the report from Madrid for the first time regarding the findings, DNA findings, for Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact date, but I think it was after about a month or a month and a half. There is a document where we can find the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal received this on the 15th of February, 2002, did you maybe receive it at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I think it was approximately at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The samples were taken to Madrid sometime in November 2001. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know when identification of those bodies was completed? Feel free to use your notes, if they can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I spoke a moment ago about the process of identification, and I said it was a complex process. Identification did not focus just on location number 1; it also encompassed other locations. And as ICMP reports arrived in my hands, they came in gradually -- just a second. On the 7th of May, 2003, on the 22nd of July, 2003, and then the 15th of October, 2003, and 3rd December 2003, we completed the first repatriations after completed identification. And these reports cover persons identified from both Batajnica 1 and Batajnica 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see from your notes when the persons from the Berisha family were identified?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Granit Berisha, father's name Besim, he was included in that first repatriation on the 7th of May. That's one Berisha --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was 2003?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then Genz Berisha, father's name Besim, repatriated at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's approximately that interval, or later?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution showed to you their document number P167, and on page 5 we saw those charred sleepers. Do you know if the conclusion has been made as to whether the sleepers had been brought from Kosovo or they were placed intact together with the bodies in Batajnica and then burned?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: We did not do that sort of analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of June, 2001, you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor regarding Radonjic Lake, but you were not asked about this at all today. So with your leave, I would like to ask for your assistance to clarify certain matters that the Defence deems important. In addition to being a renowned expert in your field of expertise, you have been a forensic expert for a long time.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that in September 1998, Investigating Judge Radovan Gojkovic, from Pec, submitted a request to your institute to engage experts to examine the bodies found in Donje Radiste and Glodjane, Decani municipality. Do you remember that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was in 1998. And at the request of the district court in Pec and Investigating Judge Gojkovic, our institute received the request to exhume and autopsy a large number of bodies that were found and seen near the canal in Radonjic Lake.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that the regular procedure for you to be engaged?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the only procedure according to which I was engaged, that is, on the orders of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that in the report or in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are using the witness statement from 5 June 2001, and that's 6D96.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It may be that it's in the statement of the next witness, but it's not in the statement we have for this witness, I don't think anyway, unless you can identify the paragraph. In any event, carry on. I just wanted to see where it was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to help you and I'll ask the registrar to put on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I don't need to see it, Mr. Lukic. It was just in case I was missing something in the report in front of me. But I don't, in fact, think I am, so please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On 11 September 1998, a MUP jeep took you to Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where did you set out from, Belgrade or some location in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I think we departed from Belgrade, from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From your experience, would you be able to tell us, is it correct that the investigating judge, in his order, clearly defines obligations of all authorities in the course of exhumations and post mortems specifically, it is clearly stated which authority carries the team for conducting post mortems, who secures the locations, who provides conditions for work, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In the order of the court it is most frequently stated that a team of experts from certain institutions is thereby established and there is an agreement with members of the team. Their assignments are specified. The order states usually that the investigating judge would be present and that he would organise the location in such a way that all persons present there would be under judicial jurisdiction. And it is stated who would assist in technical, logistical terms, who would organise transport, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the MUP does most of the supporting work, such as creating photo documentation, transportation of remains, transportation of forensic experts and judges, including provision of packed lunches?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it happened in Batajnica. I have to say that, as a member of this expert team, I was responsible for the medical expert work, but MUP provided all the technical assistance. That's the way it works where we come from. The police help us with photographing, securing the location, et cetera. That's the rule and that's the way things are done today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying that the judge is the alpha and omega of the procedure, both de jure and de facto?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he has the greatest responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You submitted your reports to him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I submitted daily reports, and after the completion of the entire procedure, post mortems and exhumations, the investigating judge receives the autopsy protocols and all the documents that are found eventually. The autopsy protocol is signed by all the members of the expert team. And the objects found are inventoried and placed in the safe-keeping of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just that the record is not quite exact. We were talking about the investigating judge and the record states only "judge."

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have been told by interpreters that we are going too fast and that's why I'm going to try to make a brief pause after your answer, which will not mean that I am not happy with your answer or that I did not understand it. You addressed the investigating judge also if you need any assistance in terms of technical means or personnel.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to take you back to the moment when you were brought to Glodjane. You were shown a house there that had been used as headquarters of the KLA. Did you personally satisfy yourself, and on the basis of what indications, that it was, indeed, a house previously used by the KLA? You say in your statement - and that's paragraph 6 on page 4 of the English version and paragraph 4, page 4 of the B/C/S version - that it was obvious to you from the red and black colouring on certain parts of the building and the KLA sign that you saw on the flag mast.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, those were the clues indicating precisely that. But as to a confirmation that it, indeed, housed some sort of headquarters, I received it from an official of the German embassy who was in Pristina at the time and who visited us in Djakovica, where we were performing the expertise on the victims, who told us that he had been locked up there for a while until his identity was established. But I really cannot tell you the name of that diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I rise just to ask if this is -- the reference to the statement, is this a reference to 6D99, the statement dated the 10th of April, 2006?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The reference is to 6D96, although in the system it might be 6D97 by mistake. Not the photos, but the other 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hopefully it will be corrected. I would kindly ask now to have 6D97, photos, on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Dunjic, we should shortly see on the screen photographs that we procured from a book, and they should relate to the time when you were in that location. Is that the canal that we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the canal. Those two photographs were taken from the direction of Radonjic Lake, and the place where the canal narrows down faces Donji Radiste and Glodjane. That's the concrete part of the canal. And the second photograph is something that I saw with my own eyes when I was on the location. We see two bodies next to the right-hand edge, depending on where you’re looking from, two bodies that were floating and that were later found in the earth-covered part of the canal, because this is the concrete part. Out of the concrete part there is a waterfall and then follows an earthen part, that is to say the natural canal, draining into Radonjic Lake. There were heavy rainfalls at the time, and flooding, and these two bodies and I don’t know how many.. a number of them were found later in the natural canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next photograph on this set. In order not to waste time, I would, in fact, like us to see page 6, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Most of the bodies that you found on that occasion were, in fact, at the end of this concrete part of the canal and at the beginning of the earthen part.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's where you found most of the body parts.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the vicinity of the site where the bodies were found is also a barn for livestock, 500, 600 metres away.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I think it was a bit closer, around 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the bottom part show the inside of that structure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: When we got to that location, we toured it, and there is a set of photographs made at the beginning. And as we were organising ourselves, how and when we should begin to work, we went to this farm that used to have these barns. In one of these we found pieces of wire, electrical wiring, the thickness of a finger, coiled around those metal bars, and they had a little noose in them. There were five or six such nooses. When we finished examining the bodies found near the concrete part of the canal and in the natural canal, and knowing that a large number of persons had gone missing in that period in 1998, the appearance of the nooses and everything that we saw on this farm indicated that some of the victims had maybe been bound, tied, in this location. And later, that turned out to be true. And remember, I'm speaking on our behalf, as experts. Two or three weeks later, near this farm but on the other side, not on the side of the canal, another five or four bodies were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you find on some bodies lengths of wire around the neck?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Next to some bodies that we found in the concrete canal, we did find lengths of this kind of wire, but we also found a large length of barbed wire that was around --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to show us the next photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is it, this is the wire I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of wire is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: That's barbed wire used for fencing, with a sliding noose on one end - we see that on the left-hand side - and strands of long black hair, the same hair that was found on one of the female victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it the case that during the exhumation there was shooting in the vicinity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: We didn't know who was shooting, but we were forced to work only up to early afternoon in order to be able to return to Djakovica from that location with security escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were lots of civilians in Djakovica who were interested in the exhumations and the results.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Some of them were from all of Kosovo and even from outside of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Those people had come to find their relatives who had been abducted before.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among the civilians who had come to see their relatives, there were Serbs and Albanians alike.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was not safe for civilians to stay longer in Djakovica after 1700 hours, so they were forced to return and come back the next day.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There were many civilians who had come to identify members of their families, but you found that among the discovered bodies there were none of their relatives, in many cases.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. We were unable to find persons that would even remotely correspond to those we had examined in detail, photographed together with clothes and anthropological findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude the number of the missing persons was much higher than the number of bodies found?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. From the number of relatives who came, we could conclude that the number of missing persons was much, much higher than the number of bodies we found near the canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Out of the 39 persons you found - and you indicated that was the smallest number - you identified only 12. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any rumours or things mentioned among the members or relatives who had come there, saying that Albanians were afraid to possibly identify some of their relatives, fearing the reprisals of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm now talking about a physician and an expert who worked on this. If we thought that a given person recognised clothing of, say, his brother, that person couldn't confirm that, indeed, that was his brother. That's why some other family members came who would also deny that that was the person, but our impression was that they, indeed, recognised certain items of clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the atmosphere, the feeling among the people who waited there to recognise some of the bodies found?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: There were different emotions. And when I say that, I mean that those people were greatly depressed, some of them afraid that they were going to be the ones to find bodies of their relatives. And some, in addition to all the desperation that was on their backs, still managed to be even slightly glad to be able to recognise some of the missing persons of their family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You wanted to carry out the autopsies on the site, but you concluded that that was far too dangerous and you did that in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Our initial intent was to do that on site, but since we could hear sporadic firing in our environs, coming from an unknown direction, we couldn't carry out the entire autopsy procedure there. Therefore, we decided to move to Djakovica, where we established a temporary centre to carry out autopsies. We noted that in our report and we informed the judge; I believe he was even present at the particular moment when we went down into this natural canyon from which we extracted the bodies. A shell flew over our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In that area, for some 15 to 20 days prior to your arrival, was there any KLA there? Did they control the area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that; I can only convey to you what I was told. We were the first officials to enter the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Among those killed, at least among those you identified, there were both Serbs and Albanians, as well as a Roma. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The work of your team was occasionally monitored by the OSCE as well as the representatives of the United States, Russia, the United Kingdom, Greece, and Germany, including two US government representatives and another representative of the UK government. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know any of their names?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you any names off the top of my head, but I believe that Judge Gojkovic received official notification of their presence because they all had to go via the Investigative Judge Gojkovic and to ask for permission to be present during the work conducted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These foreign governments and OSCE representatives, were they told the number of the bodies found?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were, and they came at the point when we had already begun identification. Since we have this picture on the screen, I wanted to use this jog my memory. I believe there was a state department representative, and he took this photograph or another photograph in which he asked me to hold the barbed wire in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that moment, could you acquaint him with the preliminary results as to the cause of death and the identity of the victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: In the most general sense, the number of victims, in our estimate, and we could tell whether these were males or females, as well as the age of those for whom we had data, and some of the injuries which could indicate what the cause of death was. In most cases this was gun-fire and in one case it was a blade, a blade injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These were more general questions. I would like to speed things up since we are limited in time. I will use a few examples and mention a few corpses you found at the location. Do you have before you your statement from 2001?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of inquiring into the method of killing, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We think that we might establish that all the victims were tortured before they were killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the relevance of that in this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The relevance of that is that the civilian population knew about these tortures, especially the civilian population in the surrounding area, and it might bring unwanted consequences later on when this population was in the position to retaliate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not so clear on the second part of what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was in 1998 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand, but it's the relevance to the indictment that I'm anxious to establish. Let's assume you establish torture. Where does that take us in relation to this indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This incident was widely exploited by media and created certain ways of thinking about civilian population in that area, and many civilians were missing at that time that later on were established were killed or still missing. And we think civilian population might act on its own without having been guided by that -- by anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But presumably you're thinking of the Albanian civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not, about the Serbian civilian population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because of KLA torture?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Carry on with your questions on that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Dunjic, the usher handed you your statement from 2001 given on the 5th of June and a few subsequent dates. If you wish, you can refer to it, if you deem it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to start with page 8, paragraph 8 in the B/C/S; in the English, page 10, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We need a number for this, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's 6D96, which is, by mistake, marked as 6D97. Does this suffice, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just waiting for it to appear on the screen, but you carry on with your question, please. The witness has his copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Starting from this page onwards, Professor Dunjic, for the most part, you analyse the bodies, injuries, and the subsequent findings of autopsies. For example, R1, that particular body, you state there that this was a woman who was between 20 and 30 years of age. I can go body by body, but I don't think the Bench wishes to receive so many details. But if you wish, we can try and sum up everything. Is it correct that among the 39 killed there were ten women? That was my count, the count of the female bodies found.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: That is what we managed to establish with certainty as to the gender; that was at least ten women.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that the injuries on these bodies were broken arms in many cases? And can you tell us what that says? What does it testify to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I didn't make such an analysis, a summary analysis, so as to be able to confirm that. But there were such injuries among the victims as part of some other types of injuries. For example, there was a gun-shot wound to the pelvis or to the skull. Once we would establish such an injury, in addition to a broken arm or a broken rib, this would indicate that that particular victim suffered another type of injury as well; that there was a blow which was so intense that would result in such a fracture, a blunt injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In several cases there were gun-shot injuries to the pelvis. What does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, I would have to use a specific example so as to be able to explain whether the shot came from the front, from the back, from the side. That is important for a forensic expert, whether someone is being shot at from the front or from the side. Also, the route or the canal can also tell us whether the victim was standing or squatting, or in what position the person was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we assume that they were shot from up close and that they sustained a pelvis injury, what sort of a death would that be? Would that be a very difficult, long death, with a lot of suffering?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that question. That is a hypothetical question which it wouldn't be appropriate for someone who is here as an expert witness to answer, and that's already been challenged. We're dealing with facts here, and to some extent, as we've indicated, it may be appropriate to ask the witness about conclusions but not on the basis of a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to go to a part of your statement in which your conclusions are specified. Is it correct that all the bodies found were in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Among those killed, there were children as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were people who were younger than 15, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On some bodies there were traces of people being tied up.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And lengths of wire were found in the stable nearby.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have also described that, and this led us to the conclusion that there were some more people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And from their relatives, you were told that their family members had been abducted by the KLA; we have that in the statement. Did you hear from some other people as well that their relatives had been abducted by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall it precisely, but this was sort of a streak through -- or among all the cases of the Albanians recognising their relatives, the people who were brave enough to come there and to identify their family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At page 29 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Paragraph 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- page 10 in the B/C/S, and page 35, paragraph 3 in the English, Mr. Hajrushi's wife described to you how her husband had been abducted by the KLA. She also said that he had been abducted together with Jusuf Hoxha. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it now that you said it. This was the man that was in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is in your statement. I just wanted to remind you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Can you at this moment recall that almost all the people who had identifiable injuries had multiple fractures antemortem or fractures caused while they were still alive; therefore, you excluded the possibility that the fractures occurred when they fell into the canal.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since we're now dealing with your conclusions in the statement, may we conclude that almost all the people - in any case a great majority of the people found - had sustained multiple bone fractures which occurred during their lifetime? And I mean different bones, of course.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Well, it seems that I need to put my expert knowledge to use here. This means the following: The findings that were noted down in detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There may be a misunderstanding here. Unfortunately, we don't have this report. It's not in the system and we'll need to deal with this later. It doesn't appear either as 6D96 or 97, so I'm working in the dark. But is your question not based on something that is actually stated in the conclusions of the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I went through all the injuries --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and I found this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not actually stated in so many words in the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I went through all the injuries, so I'm just asking the professor if he can answer; if not, we have it in the statement but we have to go case by case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is that not something that can be done out in the courtroom, in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said something to the Court when I tried to explain why I am asking these questions about Radonjic Lake, but since I cannot testify I have to ask you. The information about the killings and the information about the circumstances of these killings, was it at that time available to the public at large?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: You mean information about the sufferings or autopsy findings?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About the suffering.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was even in the newspapers. I was even getting individual -- calls from individuals who asked me if I have any information that their relative was found, or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to your statement that you gave -- that you began giving on the 9th of March, 2003 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the system, it's 6D99, just for administrative purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: A bit more than administrative purposes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just one correction: The record says "9th of March, 2003"; it's, in fact, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you need the statement? Do you want to have it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's in English on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, it's in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Oh, no, it's in B/C/S. But still, I think that we would be moving swiftly if the witness has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- a hard copy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This statement has numbered paragraphs; it will be easy to go through it. So, in relation to paragraph 19, I would like to ask you, when you are on a site, on location, you administer the collection of evidence and you give orders to the criminal technicians of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 20, the scene-of-crime officers of the MUP photograph the bodies and the objects that you indicated to them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, some of the evidence in Dusanovac, for example, MUP officers found the evidence themselves, put it in bags, and gave it to Investigating Judge Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer of the witness because the counsel speaks too fast. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: The village is Dasinovci. It should be an "a" instead of "u". It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not a single body or body part was removed from the location without your knowledge, not even after your arrival.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment you did not know the ethnic affiliation of the victims.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude that members of the MUP did not, in any way, obstruct your work; on the contrary, they contributed to it without holding back, both according to your instructions and with the steps they took on their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: That's absolutely correct, and that was all supported by the investigating judge, Rade Gojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The examinations you carried out on the farm were strictly limited by time because of the great danger in that area.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
