utterances.text: You were also limited in terms of space and area because you were only able to examine the farm and its immediate vicinity but not the whole location.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were warned from the start that we could not go further afield because there might be mines or shooting. So we had heavy police escort for security, but we did have to inspect the site as experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You performed your work according to the rules of the profession, regardless of whom the remains belonged to - Serbs, Albanians, or any other ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. But I have to say I'm a professional, a physician, a doctor, and national affiliation has never had any influence in my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While the MUP was clearing the area behind the farm, they found another five bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said the MUP was clearing the terrain?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I heard it from them, too, and to the best of my recollection, that meant securing the site when Mr. Milutinovic was supposed to arrive at the site, and he did after our work was completed. The site had to be secured so that there should not be any danger or risk. That is why the MUP combed this wide area. And in the course of this search, those bodies were found, and we assumed those bodies existed, from what we saw at the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: MUP officers carried all the bodies found in that locality to the garage of the Pastrik Hotel, on the orders of Mr. Kemal Cindric. Could you please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I have to add, though, that he was a judge who was given powers and authorisation from the superior judge, Rade Gojkovic, who had previously conducted a case in the same location.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the ethnicity of Mr. Kemal Cindric?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can only suppose that he is an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But he is not Serb, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time it could happen that neither MUP nor the judicial authorities were able to conduct an on-site investigation, according to regular procedure, and sometimes they were unable to conduct it at all due to danger, that is, attacks from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also made personal notes from the interview with Mrs. Zoja Seferaj regarding her missing husband and son. Do you remember what she told you about her husband Misin and son Axhia and the circumstances of their killing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I would have to look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's paragraph 94.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I hesitate to object, but this is asking about what somebody told him about somebody who he performed the post mortem examination on. Although we have to give some leeway during cross-examination, and presumably the cross-examination is based on some instructions, this is going way beyond anything that could be probative or relevant to the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we don't have any other means to check claims by this Mrs. Zoja Seferaj. As you know, we cannot go to Kosovo; we cannot investigate. We are trying our best to extract any kind of information we can gather, and in this case we are trying to get something from this witness that he heard at that time from another witness. Whether it is good enough for this Court or what kind of probative value it has, it's up to the Court. But with your leave, I would like to proceed with this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me make it clear at the outset: I don't accept that you cannot go to Kosovo at all. I don't accept that you -- there is no way you can carry out investigation. But that's a separate matter from the issue you raise here. The relevance must be the first question. What is this relevant to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If this witness answers, you might see; I cannot answer instead of him, but I think that he might give us the data who killed or kidnapped these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what's the relevance of that to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The relevance is that many of the Prosecutor's witnesses claim that the OVK never kidnapped, never killed, was not present, and we think that this statement of the witness is very crucial for this case, showing us what the real nature of the KLA at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the persons named here aren't witnesses in this case, are they?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, they are not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the answer to the question doesn't appear in paragraph 94, I don't think, but you're hoping that the witness will now remember something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't know. Maybe the witness knows; maybe he does not remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we consider that this may well have relevance, depending on the answer, and we do not consider the objection that it's hearsay to be sound; therefore, we repel the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Dunjic, regarding paragraph 94 from your statement of the 9th of March, 2006, do you remember what you were told by Mrs. Zoja Seferaj regarding the death of her husband and son?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely what was said then, in 1998, what exactly she told me, but I know that, among other things, she said they had gone missing because they were kidnapped by members of the KLA and taken away. But I cannot clearly remember whether he was a civil servant at the time, whether he was employed by the state administration of the Republic of Serbia, and whether that was the reason or one of the reasons why both of them were kidnapped. And later, of course, we had occasion to identify him, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about paragraph 97 now regarding Ilira Frrokaj. What did you find out from her family? Who abducted her?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Ilira Frrokaj and Tusho Frrokaj, her husband, were both abducted at that time by members of the KLA. The explanation was that they were Catholic Albanians and they were not financially contributing to the KLA movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Axhia Seferaj and his son Misin. What were they by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Ethnic Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ilira Frrokaj and her husband?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Also Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One of those killed was Seida Ndocaj, you mentioned in paragraph 38. What is his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would only like you to answer me one question regarding paragraph 123 at the end of your statement. You were speaking about the requirements put forward by Finnish pathologists when you required their assistance with regard to the mass graves found in Glodjane. You requested their forensic medical assistance. The authorities of the Republic of Serbia agreed that the exhumation of bodies of ethnic Albanians buried in Orahovac, Gornje Obrinje and Golubac be included in this exhumation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Finnish pathologists help you with the exhumations in Glodjane, as agreed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Professor. Thank you for answering my questions. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's not been entirely easy to follow all of this as it's happening, but the reference to Glodjane, with which you introduced this back at the beginning of your cross-examination, is that a reference to a different investigation from that at Dusanovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot pronounce that other one as well. But we can ask the witness, perhaps, Your Honour, it's the easiest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the report we've been looking at, 6D99, relates to Dasinovci --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That refers to two villages but I think they have been dealt with at one instance, at that time, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you clarify that for us, Professor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we were talking about from 1998 was quite a unique case we processed. There, I mean to say that these were victims from one location next to the canal that we marked with an "R"; then, there were victims from the village of Dusanovac; and the third location was marked "RE." This pertains to the victims which had been found close to the farm. We included all of them in the report and the expert findings, but they were marked differently so that we could precisely say where the bodies were found. This was quite a unique case done in the same period, in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The reference, though, that Mr. Lukic has made to exhumations in Glodjane, where the Finnish experts did not do as had been agreed, is that something separate from what you've been dealing with in relation to Dasinovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To clarify, since it is clear to me what the attorney asked, all the cases encompassed in the three marks I mentioned were termed "the Glodjane case," and that's when the Finnish experts were invited to attend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And therefore, the reference to Glodjane includes the canal next to the lake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, Mr. Lukic, 6D99 is obviously admitted, in accordance with our normal practice, and 6D97 is, because you've again referred to photographs in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Photographs are correct, 6D97 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but what's missing is 6D96.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in the system also under the number 6D97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've asked for that to be checked and I'm told it's not there. Now, if you're correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on it. If you're correct, you don't need to do anything because 6D97's been admitted, whatever it comprises; but if it's wrong, you'll need to make a filing clarifying the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Somehow there is a mistake, a technical mistake, but both documents are in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp -- oh, sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the Grahovo scene was visited by Serbian president Milutinovic in 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you say at that time what was his relationship or standing with the MUP, with the officials of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: He was the president of the state. He came to view a scene where there had been victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC
utterances.text: There is also a photograph that was published in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Professor, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is one administrative matter and I couldn't ask this witness, but I have to ask the Prosecution, because in paragraph 4 of his statement from June the 5th, 2001, he says that he handed the photo album and 56 photographs marked as B and addendum B and addendum C, that he gave to the Prosecutor's office, and we have never received those photographs. So if our learned friends can clarify whether we are going to receive this later on or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter for you to deal with informally, first of all, and involve the Trial Chamber only if there is no ready solution to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp, who will be the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. The next witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there are no complications about bringing him in, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll have the break now for half an hour. We'll resume at five past 6.00, and we will sit until ten past 7.00, since we started that bit later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Nosworthy has been suffering from a pretty heavy cold all day, and we suggested that it would be appropriate for us to continue under 15 bis in her absence. We are satisfied that that is the appropriate course, to give her a chance to recover. It may be that we will follow the same course tomorrow, depending on the circumstances. Bring in the witness now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor Aleksandric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have, as you know, before us a copy of your statement and we have also various documents to which you refer. Counsel wish to ask you additional questions, and that's the course on which we will now embark. The first counsel to ask questions of you will be, for the Prosecutor, Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good evening, Professor. Can you start by stating your name and your present --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you state your name and your present job position.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: My name is Branimir Aleksandric; father's name, Vitomir. I am a full professor at the Medical School of the University of Belgrade. I teach forensic medicine. I currently hold the position of the Head of the Forensic Medicine Institute, as of January 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the 2nd of June, 2006, did you give a statement to an investigator, an OTP investigator, in respect to your exhumation and post mortem work done at Batajnica in 2001/2002?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That statement, Your Honours, is P2412.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the statement records in detail, in some detail, the procedures you adopted. And you also say that in paragraph 17 of your statement that you made meticulous recordings of the details in the various post mortem examination reports that have appeared as a result of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, these post mortem examination reports are referred to at paragraph 16 of his statement, and they are P2413, which relates to what is referred to as Batajnica 3 -- of grave-site Batajnica 3, and P2414 to 2418 which contains the reports in respect to the grave-site known as Batajnica 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the course of your work at Batajnica, you also examined sites known as Batajnica 4, Batajnica 6, and Batajnica 7. Did you find anything at Batajnica 4, 6, and 7?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: To say right away that there was also Batajnica 8. At Batajnica 3, this was a mass grave; Batajnica 5, another mass grave. And I believe there was another one, although I can't recall its exact code. Some other numbers, for example, Batajnica 4, was an inter-space between Batajnica 3, the mass grave, and Batajnica 5, another mass grave. When the anthropologists used a bulldozer removing thin layers of soil, there were indications that something was there. That is why we gave it a separate number, Batajnica 4, thinking that it would result in yet another grave-site. So as soon as we would notice something, we would give it a code. As it turned out, that particular spot was not a grave; this was simply the area between numbers 3 and 5, but it remained as Batajnica 4 and there is a separate record of that. As for each of the spots from numbers 3 to 8, I signed a report which was forwarded to the investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, the individual reports in respect of the exhibits tendered through this witness are very complicated and detailed. I don't know if the Court would want me to go through any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. These will be admitted, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, first it will be counsel for General Lukic, and thereafter we'll follow the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. My name is Dan Ivetic and I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic in these proceedings. I'm going to have some questions for you today. First of all, Doctor, in your written statement that we have here from 2006, from June of 2006, at paragraph 2 of the English version, you mention that you were sent to Lake Radonjicko, in Kosovo, in September of 1998. Am I correct that eventually it was determined that the victims whose remains you were involved in examining and exhuming at that location were found to be civilians who had been killed by the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I visited Lake Radonjic for the examination of those victims. As for who had killed them, it is not up to me, as a forensic expert, to determine that but up to a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree. Now, am I correct that there were -- that Dr. Dunjic headed the team that was actually doing the autopsies and, in addition, you were -- you actually headed the team that was out in the field that actually located the bodies and the other artefacts that were uncovered at that location? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that anyone headed the team. It was teamwork. My learned friend Mr. Dunjic was at the Pastrik Hotel, I believe, and he would initiate autopsies there. For the first three, four, or five days - I don't know how many because there was a period during which we couldn't work because of the bad weather - in any case, I was on the site, trying to locate bodies. I would put them in bags and transport them, together with my escort, to the Pastrik Hotel in Djakovica. Once done with that, after three or five days, I joined the autopsies themselves, and then we worked on them all together up till the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we've heard some testimony already relating to the autopsies and the findings thereof. I'd like to ask -- focus for a moment on the fieldwork for a second, and I'm going to ask you: As part of your forensic investigation of the sites at or around Radonjic Lake in Kosovo, did your team prepare any written findings or summary?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Concerning each separate autopsy, there was an autopsy finding. Later on, a record would be made as well for identification. If I recall correctly, out of the 39 or 40 bodies in situ, by using the old standard methods, we identified 12 people. All the records were handed over to the then-investigating judge who was in charge of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand that, sir. I was actually asking about the examination of the situs, the location where the bodies were found. Am I correct that your team also prepared a record, or zapisnik, of what was uncovered at the field location?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: That is correct. I apologise, I seem to not have understood the question well. I was at out in the field for those three or five days and I kept record of what was found when and what code it was given, be it a body or a part of a body or an object. I took notes by hand, since there was nothing that I could type with. But every evening, upon my return to Djakovica, I went to the police station and they put a computer at my disposal; I wrote notes and protocols for the entire day, so every evening for that particular day. And I put them all together for all of the days, and that resulted in one single document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can ask for Exhibit 6D100 to be put on e-court, and I also have -- I have the Serbian language original in hard format, if that would be easier, since it does comprise about four, five, six pages for the witness to authenticate the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to show you what has been marked as 6D100 for identification purposes, and I'm going to ask you to take a few moments to review the Serbian hard copy and then I'm going to ask you if you recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I recognise my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And sir, is this --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Since this is my signature, this is authentic, everything stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the first question I want to ask you to answer, sir, is: Does this document appear to be the record that you compiled as part of your investigation into the site at Radonjic Lake where the remains of the bodies that you talked about earlier were discovered?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Here, you can read exactly what I stated - when we went out, at what time, what we found that day; and then on the next page you have the continuation of the record for the next day. Therefore, this is a record of the successive findings in the canal itself as well as in its environs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. If you could just offer some assistance for us as well with respect to this record. Do you recall, was it prepared at or around the time contemporaneous with the ongoing investigation, that is to say, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said, I was in the field every day, and in the evening, I would add to the existing record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just for clarification purposes, the signatures on each of the pages you'll -- there are two signatures by you on the Serbian version, and there is a date in 2006. Am I correct that you handed this document over to the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal, and that is why there is the date 2006; that, in fact, you authenticated the document the second time when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor. Just so there's no confusion as to the dates.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: First of all, I cannot recall the date, but I believe this tallies. On the left side, you can see the signature of the investigating judge who received this document. So this document was delivered to him on that day with my signature. And the date from 2006, the other date, is probably the date when I signed it as my document, when I handed it over to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it your normal operating practice and procedure to prepare such reports in the ordinary and regular course of conducting forensic investigations in the field?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Personally, I have no other practice. I never draft things based on my memory or sketches alone, precisely so that I wouldn't forget something, mix things up, or make a mistake. I write everything down successively, and then I re-type that every evening. That principle was used at Batajnica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, thank you, Doctor. We've heard some testimony already from one of your colleagues relative to some of the material that's set forth in this record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So, at this time, Your Honour, I would ask for 6D100 to be submitted into evidence from the bar table in its entirety rather than going through viva voce with this witness the matters contained therein. It should provide some additional information and clarification for Your Honours as to what was found at the site in Radonjic, and then I'll only highlight certain parts of that and then move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any problem with that, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I would still maintain the same objection with respect to relevance, but it has been overruled so I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there was -- if you're referring to the objection that you stated to the reference to paragraph 94, I think, of the previous witness's statement, then that was to the hearsay nature of the evidence. Is that the objection you're maintaining?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it was a combined -- it was both the hearsay nature and the thin relationship between that evidence and the issues in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. The same decision will be made. We'll repel that objection and we'll give it what weight we decide is appropriate in due course. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I would like to just highlight a few more issues from your examination at Radonjic Lake before moving on. Now, first of all, in this written record that you have just identified, a note at page 6 of the English version - that would be page 6 of the English in e-court - a note explains that when the last body was found and while your entire team was in the canyon, a shell was fired at your team and struck one of the walls of the canyon. Could you give us some more details about this as to whether -- during the course of the investigation in the field, whether this was the only incident where there was threat from fire, from fire-arms, in the area of the investigative team's work.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: It is correct. Perhaps when we were at some 30 metres down, deep in the canal, because that's how high the walls were, my colleague Mr. Draganjic Minica [phoen], and the assistant who was there, as well as the police divers, while searching the canal and its environs to find bodies or parts of bodies, something flew over our heads. I didn't know what it was at the time. My colleague and myself were left standing, whereas all the policemen lay down to the ground. It didn't exactly hit the wall of the canyon, but it flew over and landed on the other bank, although quite close. Then the police told us that what exploded was a mortar shell. They could probably recognise it by the sound. "They took their professional stand," and it was only the two of us who were still on our feet. There was another incident, perhaps the next day, as we were coming out of the canyon. Since we were going through some thick bushes, we were on all fours, and Draganjic Minica came across something which seemed weird in the soil. He naively asked a policeman what it was, and the policeman was astounded. He said, "Don't move." And there were three or four anti-personnel mines there covered with some dirt. When they dug them out, they were in some metal or tin boxes, maybe Coca-Cola boxes or something similar; maybe they were cans. After that there was always a policeman ahead of us, and we followed in a straight line back to the base camp, or rather, to the truck where we put the bodies and the finds of the day so as to return them to Djakovica. Those were the only two incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Doctor. And now with respect to the work that was conducted at the site, am I correct that, during the course of any -- and not only of that forensic exhumation, but is it also the standard operating practice at the time, and currently, for the investigative judge to be the person in charge of the same and with absolute authority over all the personnel participating in the investigation, that is to say, the person with the most responsibility?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Certainly. In principle, in our country, the investigating judge leads the entire proceedings. We, as forensic experts, are only a part of that procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in that sense, am I correct that the exhumations at Batajnica followed this same model?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now, based on your knowledge and experience, am I correct that the police, once the investigative judge has taken over the investigation and ordered any type of on-site examination or exhumation, that the police are then tasked with providing security for the transport of the team, security of the location and personnel at the site, and the crime technicians, who are then directed by the forensic personnel to record everything that is being undertaken?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I think you misstated it a bit. I don't know what that relates to, my part of the job in Djakovica or Radonjic Lake or in Belgrade, at the Batajnica location. Because if we are talking about the Radonjic Lake, we slept in Pastrik Hotel, in Djakovica, and below, in the underground garage, we conducted post mortems. And, of course, we couldn't move around on our own there. The police would take us to the location and take us back. And certainly, at that time, when there was a lot of shooting, it was an armed escort. And that's also the reason why we finished our work before dusk - you can see it in the papers - around 16, 1700 hours. As for Batajnica, we had police logistical support, if I can put it that way, inasmuch as the very compound of Batajnica we were assigned one member of the anti-terrorist unit who helped us bring food, wash dishes. It sounds a bit funny now, but the same man drove a tractor to carry the bodies to the tunnel once we have done our analysis, and the same man helped us if we needed new pipes or something, a spare part from the fridge. We had an understanding with the investigating judge that we would go to the Batajnica location every day from our homes, in our own cars, and the court would cover the expenses of that transportation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir, we'll get to the Batajnica exhumation in just a second. I'd like to finish up, for the sake of clarity and continuity, with the exhumations performed at Radonjic Lake first, and then I'll move on to Batajnica and we'll complete all the matters that need to be discussed with respect to Batajnica. Now, sir, with respect to the work that was performed at Lake Radonjic, did the forensic data and evidence visible at the scenes where the bodies were located indicate that the victims had, in fact, died at those locations?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: You see, when you have a decomposing, rotting body, it's difficult to establish even a cause of death, let alone whether the persons found their death in the same location. Everybody knows of the refrigerator truck case in the Danube that came first and that the bodies from the refrigerator truck were later buried into the ground. And the forensic experts performed post mortems on buried bodies. How do you think a forensic can tell the cause of death in totally decomposed bodies taken out from the ground? Those people in the truck could have died of suffocation because the truck was closed; they could have been alive when they sank --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, the question doesn't relate to the refrigerated truck; it relates to the lake at Radonjic. If the answer is no, just give us that answer, please, rather than a detailed explanation. Because if counsel does want more information, he will ask for more. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I understand. I thought I would just give you an introductory explanation for a specific answer; namely, it is difficult to say whether all the bodies we found at Radonjic Lake found their death there or elsewhere and then were transported and thrown into the canal. It is also questionable into which part of the canal they were thrown because the water had carried them. When we came there, we saw some bodies in one spot in the canal. And on the third day, I think, the skies seemed to open and it started pouring, and when that rainfall stopped, we found those same bodies hundreds of metres further down. It is logical to assume that, from the moment when they got there until the moment our team arrived, there had been other instances of calamitous weather. That canal is not a little puddle; it was a great mass of water, especially after rainfalls.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir, just one more follow-up on that and then I will move on. Did you find any forensic artefacts or evidence that any of the -- that indicated that any of the bodies had, in fact, been lined up against the canal wall and shot, in the Radonjic Lake instant?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: I think in this record that I kept on the spot - we are still talking about Radonjic Lake, if I understood you well - at least in the Serbian version, on page 3, in paragraph 1, the following description is found: "On the concrete wall that delimited the canal, on the external side where there is soil, we found a lot of damage consistent with projectiles." And also below, a mass of gravel that was slightly different from the other gravel; namely, it was not overgrown, not even a little, by grass. There were no patches of fresh grass, so we suspected there could be something below that gravel. We found bodies, and they were marked on the spot. You see that on the record. F14, 15, and maybe some other identifications. I don't know if we found two or three or how many. So on the basis of the entire picture on the spot, on the basis of those circumstances and the post mortems performed later, we could conclude that those two or three persons died there from gun-fire and that they were later buried and covered with gravel. Relevant photo documentation was also provided to the investigating judge, and there is underlying evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, in regards to the autopsies that were performed, we've heard testimony that there was a large media reporting of the event. Do you recall if you, yourself, witnessed any large amounts of civilian persons who came to the Hotel Pastrik to try and find out what was going on and whether any of the bodies that had been uncovered were friends or relatives?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: You see, this is the procedure: When we finished the whole procedure, from finding the bodies and finishing the first post mortems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sir, it would be helpful if you'd go directly to the question and answer it rather than tell us the procedure. It's a very specific question. Were you involved in meeting people who came looking for the bodies of their friends or relatives? The answer must be yes or no, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, if that's the answer you're looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And now counsel can ask you for more information if he wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, would it be fair to say that the general atmosphere within Djakovica at that time, particularly the local population that was around the Hotel Pastrik, showed a great concern for what had been discovered and the victims and the potential threat posed by whomever had killed the persons at that location?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I had no idea what the atmosphere was outside the hotel for the simple reason that we had our hands full with our job on post mortems. However, when we completed post mortems and started identifications, we came into contact with those unfortunate families, and with their assistance, we had to try to identify the bodies. And that was the first time we came into contact with those people who had missing family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now move on to ask you some questions with respect to the Batajnica exhumation investigation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, we've tried to set some guidance for the use of time, and I'm very reluctant to get involved in this sort of discussion, but this cross-examination doesn't seem to be observing these --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- these guidelines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I may answer that, Your Honour. The Prosecution provided us with an estimation of time for this witness. They were going to lead him an hour and a half. This morning, when I talked with the lead counsel, Mr. Hannis, I was advised that they were revising that to 45 minutes. I have cut down my cross-examination to be 35 to 40 minutes, but obviously they went five minutes with their direct. I can tell you exactly now that I have five more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wasn't aware of that. It would be helpful to the Bench to know what's actually happening when the guidelines are clearly not being followed. So I hope that practice will be followed in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I will definitely follow that in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not confined to the Defence conduct either; it's happening on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, as you've heard we have time constraints, I would like to just ask you briefly, as I indicated, five questions relating to Batajnica. I believe you had already started talking about this previously with respect to the bodies that were from the refrigerated lorry. I'd like to ask you: Generally speaking, about all of the bodies that were exhumed, am I correct that, due to the advanced stage of putrefaction and decomposition of the remains, the precise cause of death could not be ascertained to a requisite degree of medical certainty for the bulk of the remains, that is to say, for most, if not all, of the remains that were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: First of all, all of the bodies were in an advanced state of putrefaction, absolutely all of them; some were even pure skeletons. In principle, when you perform post mortems on such bodies, whether they were exhumed or found in a state of decomposition, a simple autopsy of a decomposed body cannot give you a definitive cause of death. That is a job for further expertise which will use the post mortems, evidence from the on-site investigation, clothing, objects found on the body, and other factors, to provide an indication of the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you've actually answered my next question as well. Just let me ask you this, sir: In your statement you give the opinion that the bodies that had been exhumed, at least from Batajnica 3, I believe it was, that you had examined, showed evidence of having been exposed to fire, And you conclude that the -- that the bodies had -- that there had been an attempt to burn the bodies at that location. Could you please expound upon that and give us the bases for your conclusion that there had been an attempt to burn the bodies at the Batajnica 3 location.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: First of all, I think it was also the case in the second mass grave. I don't know the exact number, but everything is in our records. And as for the record and why we came to the conclusion that the bodies were burnt, it's simply that the tires below and on top of the bodies were burned and post mortems also established traces of fire primarily on the bones but also on the soft tissues and, of course, on the clothing covering the bodies, and even in the personal documents found in the clothing, below the clothing, tucked under the belt, et cetera. So we had clear evidence of the bodies' exposure to fire. And since the bodies themselves were found next to tires which undoubtedly were incinerated, there was no other conclusion but that the bodies were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you indicated that there was the burnt tires that were there. Were there other indications to show that, in fact, the burning had been attempted physically there at the Batajnica -- were any of the soil -- any evidence in the soil or other artefacts that indicated that the attempts to burn the bodies had been conducted physically at that location rather than anyplace else?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR ALEKSANDRIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we also found charred or burned planks. But I repeat once again: It's all in our records. I cannot remember any other details. I remember only tires and planks and, of course, the burned bodies and clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Aleksandric. I apologise for rushing you through this, but we did have time constraints. I thank you for your assistance today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No re-examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Professor, that does complete your evidence. As I explained at the beginning, we have your written statement, and, as counsel indicated at the outset, it has with it a large number of very carefully prepared documents dealing in great detail with these events which are all before the Trial Chamber for their consideration. We are grateful to you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence, and you are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, and good evening to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The next witness is P -- is K62. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 72. A few minutes ago I made inquiries as to his availability and I was told that an estimation had been made and he had been transported back to the hotel. Therefore, I told them that there was no point in going back for him, if it was anticipated that we might finish a few moments before 7.10. Indeed, there would have been no point in going back to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I agree with that; the mistake was not keeping him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand the witness is there, Mr. Stamp, so shall we bring him in?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. I'm trying to contact my colleague to see if he could come down. I'm wondering if it's really feasible at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, yes, every minute counts, I'm afraid, in this trial and we should get started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. You are known to us in the court as K72, and that's the reference we will have to use for you throughout your evidence. Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. The Court has before it a statement you gave, which we have read; that was given in October 2005. Nevertheless, you're here to answer further questions to supplement the information in the statement or clarify things or possibly to be challenged about things that are in there. I don't know exactly what questions you will be asked, but you will be asked questions along these lines. Now, the first person to examine you will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness is K72. Yes, we have a pseudonym sheet, which is being printed out at that moment, I hope. This witness's evidence, Your Honour, pertains to paragraph 75(h) in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he's 92 ter, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is listed as live and 92 ter, I believe on the witness notification from last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, first of all, I would like to begin by handing you a document. If you can look at that and read it to yourself and please advise us if that information is correct, as far as your personal details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is Exhibit P2392, I believe. We'd tender that at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May that be received under seal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, I would next like to show you Exhibit 2390. Do you recall giving a statement to an investigator from the ICTY last year, on the 26th of October? I'm sorry, did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you recall having given a statement to an investigator from the ICTY last year, on the 26th of October?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could, I have a hard copy that I could hand the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you came to court here this evening, did you have a chance to review that written statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in reviewing that you noted a couple of minor changes that you indicated to us, we Prosecutors, who put it in a supplemental information provided to the Defence the day after you were interviewed. Are you otherwise satisfied that the information contained in that written statement is true and accurate, to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Court now that the answers you gave at that time are the same answers you would give now if you were asked those same questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: Yes, the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd like to tender 2390 at this time, also under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That will be admitted under seal also subject to the production, as soon as possible, of a redacted version.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will do so, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to deal with the changes --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I intended to do that as I went through his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as long as you identify them as you come to them, since it's helpful to have them clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. There are only a couple of minor details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement at paragraph 10, you talk about how, when the NATO bombing started, you began to work for the VJ as a civilian. Can you tell the Court how you first came to be tasked to do work for the army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: In a hotel in Djakovica, called Pastrik, an officer came up to me. They addressed him as lieutenant-colonel, I don't know his name, and told me that I should report to the barracks the next day in order to do something for the army with some equipment. I did do that and that's how it started.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the time that happened you were working for a private company you called Bokshi, and I understand you worked as an excavator operator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: Yes, it was called Bokshi by the surname --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it the entire company of Bokshi that was asked to help the army or was it just you individually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: I don't know whether a request had been made to him, but I did operate his machine. He brought the machine to the MUP quarters and that's where I operated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you paid for the work you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: While I worked at the barracks on Cabrat hill for the army, I dug roads, trenches for the digging in of combat equipment, embankments. And they gave me per diem; I don't remember how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How often were you paid? Did you get paid every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: I think every fortnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you were working for them, how did you get to and from the job? Did you drive yourself or were you transported by someone else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: No. I was driven there and back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In what kind of vehicle, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: I think it was some sort of jeep, olive-grey-green, by a military person. Whether it was a soldier or an officer, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 11 you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before moving to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your question about how you were paid. Who actually paid you when you were doing this work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody who held the treasury who paid out money to everybody, including officers. I heard that everybody had the same per diem, the soldiers and us. I think the same person paid out the money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, you can find a suitable time whenever.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One last question on that. Did you have to sign anything when you received your payment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K72
utterances.text: I did not sign anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This would be a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, K72, we have to conclude the proceedings for the day at this stage, and we will resume your evidence tomorrow; that will be tomorrow afternoon at 2.15. You need to be back here ready to resume evidence at 2.15 tomorrow. Meanwhile - and this is very important - now that you are in the position of giving your evidence, you must not discuss your evidence with anyone at all, and that means either the evidence you've already given or the evidence that you may yet give tomorrow. So tonight and until you come back tomorrow you can discuss whatever you like with whomsoever you like, except the evidence in this case; that is absolutely off-limits in your discussions. So we will see you again tomorrow at 2.15. The usher will now show you the way from the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we adjourn now until 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
